title: Tell me about a disagreement you had with your manager
prompt: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a manager or someone responsible for a group or task. Explain what concerned you, how you chose to respond, and what happened. Use an example you are comfortable discussing; you do not need to disclose private or distressing details.
blurb: Conflict with manager (senior): can they challenge up with candor and professionalism — and handle either outcome maturely?

rubric.label: Situation & the disagreement
rubric.description: Explains the disagreement, relevant facts and why the issue mattered without requiring high financial stakes or a formal reporting relationship.

rubric.label: Willingness to challenge up
rubric.description: Explains a proportionate way to raise or document the concern, including an alternative channel if direct discussion was unsafe or unsuitable.

rubric.label: Specific contribution and decisions
rubric.description: Describes their specific response, supporting reasoning, attention to other relevant information and an appropriate boundary or escalation.

rubric.label: Outcome and evidence
rubric.description: Describes the response and consequences honestly, including unresolved disagreement; agreement, obedience and preserving a relationship are not required outcomes.

rubric.label: Reflection & professionalism
rubric.description: Explains what they learned about raising concerns, authority, evidence and when to seek support or use a different channel.

rubric.label: Clear, relevant communication
rubric.description: Makes the relevant situation, reasoning and contribution understandable in any clear order. No required STAR structure, pronouns, performance of confidence or emotional tone.

reference.scenario: Explore disagreement with someone coordinating or supervising work, study or a community activity. The concern can involve priorities, quality, fairness or safety. Assess the reasoning and response within the circumstances, without assuming that direct confrontation or compliance is always appropriate.
model_points: States the disagreement and separates observations from assumptions about the other person.
Explains their responsibility and the consequences that mattered.
Chooses a suitable communication or reporting channel; seeking support, documenting or bypassing the person may be justified.
Engages with relevant counterevidence without having to excuse unsafe conduct or suppress a legitimate concern.
Describes an agreement, refusal, escalation or unresolved outcome accurately; winning agreement is not the scoring target.
Reflects on how to raise future concerns while respecting safety, ethics and applicable responsibilities.

probes.question: What was the specific concern you wanted addressed?
What made that channel appropriate in this situation?

probes.trigger: candidate gives only the other person’s response
probes.question: What did you do after that response?

red_flags: Knowingly misrepresents the issue or evidence to undermine another person.
Threatens or retaliates against someone raising a legitimate concern.
Claims that an authority’s instruction removes the need to consider an identified safety or ethical concern.
follow_ups: What would make a different reporting channel appropriate?
What did you learn about the evidence needed to explain your concern?
reference.exemplar_answer: Illustrative example only; it is not a required setting, answer order or achievement standard. A volunteer coordinator proposed dropping an accessibility check to save time. I explained which part of the activity could become inaccessible and asked whether we could reduce a different task. When we could not agree, I brought the concern to the event lead using the approved process. The lead kept the check and reduced the activity’s scope. I learned to make the effect on participants concrete while using support when needed.
reference.assessment_contract: Assess the selected competency from concrete job-relevant evidence. Examples from paid work, study, volunteering, caregiving, informal work, military service and community activities are equally eligible when relevant. A modest example is sufficient if it shows the competency; employer prestige, formal title and financial scale are not criteria. Accept qualitative or quantitative outcomes supported by the account, including partial or unsuccessful outcomes. Do not require a numeric metric, STAR order, particular pronouns, composure, enthusiasm or a particular communication style. Identify personal contribution by meaning while preserving credit to others. Assess intelligibility and relevance, not accent, fluency, verbosity, visible emotion, disability or private circumstances. Mark genuinely missing evidence not assessed; do not infer poor competence or dishonesty from an absent example. A clearly labeled hypothetical may be discussed as situational practice but must not count as demonstrated past experience. Respect scope of practice, authorization, safety and ethical duties; pausing, declining, reporting or escalating can be sound judgment. Never require obedience, direct confrontation, unpaid overwork or successful persuasion regardless of the circumstances.
